lessons.title: Identifying Through-Hole Components
lessons.body: Through-hole components are the traditional electronic parts with long metal leads that go through holes in a circuit board. You will see them in almost every repair job across Africa, from radios in Accra to solar charge controllers in Nairobi. Start by sorting them into groups: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, ICs, connectors, and switches. Resistors are small cylinders with coloured bands. A 10k ohm resistor has bands brown, black, orange, gold. Capacitors come in two main types: ceramic discs (small, no polarity) and electrolytic cans (larger, with a white stripe marking the negative lead). Diodes are black cylinders with a silver band at one end â that band marks the cathode. Transistors look like little black half-cylinders with three legs; the flat side shows the part number like BC547. ICs are black rectangular chips with 8, 14, or 16 legs. Connectors are plastic headers or screw terminals. Switches are mechanical. Use a cheap digital multimeter set to continuity or resistance to confirm values. For example, a good 100 ohm resistor reads about 100 ohms. A bad capacitor may read zero or infinite. Always check the part number printed on the component. In many African markets, components are salvaged from old TVs and computers, so markings may be faded. Clean the part with a cloth and use a magnifying glass. Keep a notebook listing each componentâs name, value, and polarity. This habit saves hours during assembly. Remember: polarity matters for electrolytic capacitors, diodes, LEDs, and ICs. Non-polar parts like resistors and ceramic capacitors can go either way. Practice identifying 20 random components from a mixed bag until you can name them in under 10 seconds each.

lessons.title: Component Preparation and Lead Forming
lessons.body: Before you insert any component, you must prepare its leads. This step prevents damage and ensures a proper fit. Start with a pair of small flush cutters and a lead-forming tool or a simple pair of round-nose pliers. For resistors and diodes, bend the leads to match the hole spacing on your board. A common spacing is 0.4 inches (10 mm). Hold the component body with one hand and use pliers to bend the leads 90 degrees downward. Do not bend right at the body â leave a small gap of about 1 mm to avoid cracking the seal. For capacitors, especially electrolytics, keep the leads straight unless the board requires a specific bend. Clean the leads with fine sandpaper or a pencil eraser to remove oxidation. In humid African climates, oxidation is common, and dirty leads cause bad solder joints. If leads are too long, trim them to about 5 mm below the board after insertion â but wait to trim until after soldering. For ICs, never bend the legs. Instead, use a DIP insertion tool or gently straighten them on a flat surface. If a leg is bent, use tweezers to realign it. For transistors, identify the emitter, base, and collector before forming. A BC547 has a flat side; the middle leg is base, the left is collector, right is emitter when viewed from the front. Form leads to fit the boardâs triangle pattern. Always wear safety glasses when cutting leads â flying metal can injure your eyes. Use a lead-forming jig if available; otherwise, a small vice and pliers work fine. After forming, place all prepared components in a clean tray sorted by value. This preparation step may take 10 minutes per 20 components, but it speeds up assembly and reduces rework. In many African workshops, technicians skip this step and later struggle with misaligned parts. Donât be that technician.

lessons.title: Inserting and Securing Components
lessons.body: Insertion is where your prepared components meet the board. Start with the lowest-profile parts: resistors, diodes, and small ceramic capacitors. Place the board on a flat surface or in a holder. Insert each componentâs leads through the correct holes. For polarized parts, match the positive lead to the square pad or the hole marked with a plus sign. On most boards, the square pad is positive for electrolytic capacitors and the round pad is negative. For diodes, the banded end goes to the pad marked with a line or a K. For ICs, align the notch or dot with the notch on the silkscreen. Push the component down until it sits flush against the board â no gap larger than 1 mm. If a component stands off the board (like power resistors), use a spacer or leave a 2-3 mm gap for cooling. Once inserted, bend the leads outward at about 45 degrees to hold the part in place. This is called clinching. Do not bend them flat against the board â that makes rework difficult. For multi-lead parts like ICs, insert one row first, then gently push the other row in. If a lead wonât go, do not force it â check for a bent leg or wrong hole. Use a small screwdriver to guide leads. After all components are inserted, flip the board over and check that each part is seated properly. You can use a piece of foam or a soft cloth to hold components in place while flipping. Secure large or heavy components with a small dab of silicone or hot glue after soldering, especially in high-vibration environments like solar installations in dusty areas. In African workshops, a common mistake is inserting tall components first, which makes it hard to reach shorter ones. Always work from short to tall. Practice inserting 10 resistors, 2 capacitors, and 1 IC on a scrap board until you can do it without thinking.

lessons.title: Soldering Through-Hole Components
lessons.body: Soldering is the heart of electronics assembly. You need a soldering iron with a fine tip, 60/40 or lead-free solder (0.8 mm diameter is ideal), a wet sponge or brass wool, and a fume extractor or small fan. Set your iron to 350Â°C for leaded solder or 380Â°C for lead-free. Let it heat for 5 minutes. Clean the tip on the sponge, then apply a small amount of solder to tin the tip. For each joint, follow this method: touch the iron tip to both the pad and the component lead at the same time. Count one second. Then feed solder into the joint â not onto the iron tip. The solder should melt and flow around the lead and pad like a small volcano. Remove solder first, then remove the iron. The whole process should take 2-3 seconds. A good joint is shiny, smooth, and concave. A bad joint looks dull, blobby, or ball-shaped. For African learners, practice on a scrap board with 20 resistors. Common problems: too little heat (cold joint), too much solder (bridge), or moving the component before solder cools. If you see a bridge between two pads, use solder wick or a desoldering pump to remove excess. Keep your tip clean every 3-4 joints. Do not use too much pressure â you can lift pads. For ground planes or large copper areas, you may need a higher wattage iron (40W or more). After soldering, trim the leads flush with the board using flush cutters. Hold the lead so it doesnât fly. Inspect each joint with a magnifying glass. In many African settings, power fluctuations can affect iron temperature; use a surge protector or a voltage stabilizer. If you are soldering in a humid environment, keep the board dry. Practice until you can solder 30 joints in 5 minutes with 90% perfect. That speed and quality will get you hired.

lessons.title: Inspecting Through-Hole Solder Joints
lessons.body: Inspection is not optional â it is how you catch defects before they cause failures. After soldering, let the board cool for 2 minutes. Use a magnifying glass (10x) and bright light. Start by checking each joint visually. A good joint has a shiny, smooth, concave fillet that wets both the pad and the lead. The solder should look like a tiny volcano. A cold joint is dull, lumpy, and may have a crack around the lead. A cold joint often results from insufficient heat or dirty surfaces. A solder bridge is a blob of solder connecting two adjacent pads â this causes short circuits. Use a multimeter set to continuity to check for bridges between neighbouring pads. A disturbed joint looks like a frozen drip â it happens if the component moved while solder was cooling. A blowhole or pinhole indicates trapped gas or contamination. For each defect, mark it with a small piece of tape or a marker. Then check component placement: is the part flush? Are polarized parts oriented correctly? Look for leads that are too long or too short. Use a dental pick or tweezers to gently tug each lead â a good joint will not move. If it moves, itâs a cold joint. In African repair shops, a common defect is insufficient solder on ground pads because the copper plane sucks heat away. Reheat those joints with a hotter iron and add a little solder. Also check for splashes of solder on the board â remove them with a brush. After inspection, clean the board with isopropyl alcohol and a toothbrush to remove flux. Flux residue can cause corrosion over time, especially in humid coastal areas like Mombasa or Lagos. A clean board is easier to inspect and more reliable. Document your findings: count the number of defects per 100 joints. A good target is less than 2 defects per 100. If you find more, review your soldering technique. Inspection takes 5 minutes for a small board, but it saves hours of troubleshooting later.

lessons.title: Rework and Touch-Up of Through-Hole Assemblies
lessons.body: Rework means fixing defects found during inspection. Touch-up means improving a joint that is not perfect but not yet failed. You need a soldering iron, solder sucker or solder wick, flux pen, tweezers, and a heat-resistant mat. Start by identifying the defect. For a cold joint, reheat the joint with the iron and add a tiny amount of fresh solder. The flux in the new solder will clean the joint. Hold the iron for 1-2 seconds, then remove. For a solder bridge, use solder wick: place the wick over the bridge, press with the iron, and the wick will absorb excess solder. Alternatively, use a solder sucker â heat the bridge and quickly suck the molten solder. For a component that needs replacement, first remove solder from all pads using wick or sucker. Then gently pull the component out with tweezers while heating one lead at a time. Do not force it â you can lift pads. If a pad lifts, you may need to run a jumper wire to the next component. For touch-up, if a joint looks dull but is electrically good, add a little flux and reheat. Do not add more solder unless needed. After rework, clean the area with isopropyl alcohol. Always test the board after rework with a multimeter to ensure no shorts and correct continuity. In African workshops, rework is common because components are often salvaged. Practice rework on a scrap board: create 10 cold joints, then fix them. Time yourself â a skilled technician can fix a cold joint in 10 seconds. Remember: never rework a joint more than 3 times â repeated heating can damage the pad and the component. If a pad is damaged, use a small wire to bridge to the nearest connected point. Keep your iron tip clean and tinned. After rework, re-inspect the joint. A good rework is invisible â it looks like a factory joint. Finally, log what you fixed and why. This helps you improve your assembly process and avoid repeating mistakes.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Through-Hole Component Assembly

Through-hole assembly remains the backbone of electronics manufacturing across Africa â from small workshops in Kumasi and Nairobi to contract manufacturers supplying solar inverters, radio transmitters, and agricultural sensor boards. Unlike surface-mount work, through-hole assembly is forgiving of modest equipment, tolerates high-vibration environments, and produces mechanically robust joints that survive heat, dust, and humidity. For an African SME, mastering through-hole assembly is a direct route to revenue: repair contracts, low-volume production runs, and prototype services for universities and agritech startups.

This practical reference condenses the six lessons in this module into a single working document. Use it on the bench, print it for the workshop wall, or adapt it into a training handout for apprentices.

1. Identifying Through-Hole Components

Through-hole parts are classified by function and by lead count. Resistors, capacitors, and diodes are axial or radial; ICs come in DIP (dual in-line package); connectors and relays are typically large and mechanically stressed. In the African market, component sourcing is the first business constraint: counterfeit electrolytics and recycled ICs are common. Build a verified supplier list and inspect incoming stock with a multimeter and capacitance meter before accepting a consignment.

Table 1: Common through-hole component types and African market sourcing notes
Component Typical Marking Orientation Sensitive? Local Sourcing Note
Carbon film resistorColor bandsNoWidely available; buy 1% metal film for instrumentation work.
Electrolytic capacitorValue, voltage, polarity stripeYes â polarityCounterfeits common; verify ESR and capacitance on receipt.
Ceramic capacitor3-digit code (e.g., 104)NoReliable; check voltage rating for solar/automotive use.
Diode (1N400x)Part number, bandYes â cathode bandCheap and plentiful; test forward drop.
LEDFlat side = cathodeYesVerify color and forward voltage before assembly.
DIP ICPart number, pin-1 notch/dotYesRecycled parts common; test in socket first.
Transistor (TO-92)Part number, pinoutYesCheck pinout â TO-92 variants differ.
Relay / connectorPart numberOften yesPrefer branded parts for mains-switching duty.

2. Component Preparation and Lead Forming

Leads must be cleaned, straightened, and formed to match the hole pitch. Use lead-forming pliers or a simple jig to bend leads without stressing the component body. Oxidation on recycled leads is the leading cause of cold joints in African workshops â clean with isopropyl alcohol or a soft eraser before insertion.

3. Inserting and Securing Components

Insert components from the non-solder side, working from lowest profile to tallest. Bend leads outward at 30â45Â° to hold parts in place during soldering. For heavy parts (transformers, large relays), use mechanical fasteners or silicone adhesive in addition to solder â vibration from generators and vehicles will otherwise crack joints.

4. Soldering Through-Hole Components

Use a temperature-controlled iron at 350â370 Â°C with lead-free SAC305 or, where permitted, Sn63/Pb37. Apply heat to both pad and lead for 1â2 seconds, feed solder, then remove solder first, then iron. Target a shiny, concave fillet on both sides of the board. In humid coastal environments, use no-clean flux with adequate solids to prevent dendritic growth.

Table 2: Recommended soldering parameters for through-hole assembly
Parameter Sn63/Pb37 (leaded) SAC305 (lead-free) Source
Iron tip temperature315â345 Â°C350â370 Â°CIPC J-STD-001
Contact time (typical)2â3 s3â4 sIPC J-STD-001
Tip size (typical pad)2.4 mm chisel2.4 mm chiselManufacturer guidance
Flux typeRMA / no-cleanNo-clean, halide-freeIPC J-STD-004
Fillet appearanceShiny, concaveMatte, concaveIPC-A-610 Class 2
â  SAFETY WARNING â Lead and Flux Fumes

Leaded solder and rosin flux produce toxic fumes. Solder only in a well-ventilated area with an activated-carbon fume extractor or cross-draft fan. Wash hands thoroughly after handling leaded solder â never eat or drink at the bench. In shared workshops, keep a dedicated soldering zone away from food preparation and child-accessible areas. Store solder and flux in sealed containers; dispose of dross and used tips as hazardous waste, not general refuse.

5. Inspecting Through-Hole Solder Joints

Inspect at 5â10Ã magnification or with a loupe. Acceptable joints show a bright, concave fillet wetting both pad and lead, with lead outline visible. Reject: cold joints (dull, blobby), insufficient solder (no fillet), excess solder (convex ball), bridges between pads, disturbed joints (frosty, cracked), and lifted pads. For Class 2 and Class 3 work, follow IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria exactly â this is what export customers and telecoms operators will audit.

6. Rework and Touch-Up

Rework is a business cost, not a failure. Use a solder sucker or desoldering braid to remove excess solder; use flux-cored wire and a clean tip for touch-up. Never reheat a joint more than twice without removing and re-preparing the lead â repeated heating damages pads and components. Document every rework in a simple logbook; this becomes evidence of quality control when bidding for larger contracts.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Verify component value, polarity, and pin-1 orientation against the BOM and silkscreen before insertion.
  • Clean oxidized leads with isopropyl alcohol or a soft eraser.
  • Form leads to match hole pitch â never bend directly at the component body.
  • Insert lowest-profile parts first; secure tall or heavy parts mechanically.
  • Set iron to 350â370 Â°C for lead-free, 315â345 Â°C for leaded solder.
  • Heat pad and lead together for 1â2 s before feeding solder.
  • Inspect every joint at 5â10Ã magnification against IPC-A-610 criteria.
  • Log all rework; retrain on any recurring defect pattern.

Further Reading

  • IPC J-STD-001 â Requirements for Soldered Electrical and Electronic Assemblies
  • IPC-A-610 â Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies
  • NASA-STD-8739.3 â Soldered Electrical Connections
  • ITU â Green Standards and E-Waste Guidance for Developing Markets
  • UNIDO â Electronics Manufacturing in Developing Economies

Business takeaway: Through-hole assembly is the entry point for African electronics SMEs. It requires low capital, tolerates local supply-chain imperfections, and produces products that survive African operating conditions. Master the six steps above, document your quality control, and you can credibly bid for repair, prototype, and low-volume production contracts from agritech, telecoms, and solar companies across the continent.

quiz.q: What colour bands does a 10k ohm resistor have?
quiz.explanation: Brown (1), black (0), orange (x1000) gives 10,000 ohms or 10k.

quiz.q: Which component has a white stripe marking the negative lead?
quiz.explanation: Electrolytic capacitors are polarized and the stripe indicates the negative terminal.

quiz.q: What does the silver band on a diode indicate?
quiz.explanation: The band marks the cathode, the negative end of the diode.

quiz.q: How many legs does a BC547 transistor have?
quiz.explanation: A BC547 is a standard three-leg bipolar transistor.

quiz.q: Why should you clean component leads before soldering?
options: B) To remove oxidation for better solder flow
quiz.explanation: Oxidation prevents solder from wetting the lead, causing bad joints.

quiz.q: When forming leads, how far from the component body should you bend?
quiz.explanation: Bending too close can crack the seal or damage the component.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of clinching leads after insertion?
options: A) To make a better electrical connection
B) To hold the component in place before soldering
quiz.explanation: Clinching (bending leads outward) mechanically secures the part during soldering.

quiz.q: Which component should be inserted first on a board?
quiz.explanation: Lowest-profile parts go first so taller parts donât block access.

quiz.q: What is the correct soldering iron temperature for leaded solder?
quiz.explanation: 350Â°C is ideal for 60/40 leaded solder; higher may damage pads.

quiz.q: What does a good solder joint look like?
quiz.explanation: A shiny, concave fillet indicates proper wetting and heating.

quiz.q: How long should you apply heat to a through-hole joint?
quiz.explanation: 2-3 seconds is enough to melt solder without damaging the board.

quiz.q: What tool removes excess solder from a bridge?
quiz.explanation: Solder wick absorbs molten solder when heated over the bridge.

quiz.q: What is a cold solder joint?
options: A) A joint soldered at low temperature
B) A dull, lumpy joint with poor electrical contact
C) A joint with too much solder
D) A joint that is too shiny
quiz.explanation: Cold joints result from insufficient heat and look dull and irregular.

quiz.q: Why is flux residue harmful?
options: A) It causes corrosion over time
B) It makes the board heavier
quiz.explanation: Flux residue can be corrosive, especially in humid climates.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean a board after soldering?
quiz.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol dissolves flux without damaging components.

quiz.q: How many defects per 100 joints is a good target?
quiz.explanation: High-quality assembly aims for fewer than 2 defects per 100 joints.

quiz.q: What is the first step in rework of a cold joint?
options: B) Reheat the joint with the iron
quiz.explanation: Reheating with a small amount of fresh solder reflows the joint.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pad lifts during rework?
options: B) Run a jumper wire to the next component
quiz.explanation: A lifted pad breaks the circuit; a jumper wire restores connectivity.

quiz.q: How many times can you safely rework a joint?
quiz.explanation: Repeated heating can damage the pad and component; limit to 3 times.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fume extractor when soldering?
options: B) To remove harmful solder fumes
quiz.explanation: Solder fumes contain flux vapours that are harmful if inhaled.

quiz.q: Which component is non-polarized?
quiz.explanation: Resistors have no polarity and can be inserted either way.

quiz.q: What does a solder bridge cause?
quiz.explanation: A bridge connects two pads that should be separate, causing a short.

quiz.q: What is the recommended lead length below the board after soldering?
quiz.explanation: Leads should be trimmed flush with the solder joint to prevent shorts.

quiz.q: Why should you not force a component into holes?
options: A) It may bend leads or damage the board
B) It will change its value
quiz.explanation: Forcing can bend leads, crack pads, or break the component.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a heat sink when soldering?
quiz.explanation: Heat sinks clip onto leads to draw heat away from sensitive parts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a through-hole component?
quiz.explanation: DIP (dual in-line package) ICs have through-hole leads.

quiz.q: What is the first step in identifying a component?
options: B) Read its markings and shape
D) Test it with a multimeter
quiz.explanation: Visual inspection of markings and shape is the quickest way to identify.

quiz.q: How can you test a resistorâs value?
options: A) With a multimeter set to ohms
quiz.explanation: Colour bands give the nominal value, and a multimeter confirms it.

quiz.q: What does a continuity test check for?
options: C) Whether a circuit is complete
quiz.explanation: Continuity checks if there is a low-resistance path between two points.

quiz.q: Why is it important to log rework actions?
quiz.explanation: Logging helps identify recurring defects and improve technique.
